name: Brightness and air at the source for pads and textures
goal: Make pads bright and airy from the start (instead of boosting treble at the end): choose harmonically rich oscillators, open and key-track the filter, add octave/fifth layers, excite upper harmonics, add a quiet air-noise layer, brighten before reverb and only then a gentle shelf.

source.note: Written from established production practice to fill a library gap; no single source video.

sources.title: Sound Design - Ambient Pads and Atmospheres
Ambient Step by Step Tutorial - Techniques and Processing: Creating Ambient Environment Soundscapes
How to Use White Noise in Your Music

theory: Perceived brightness tracks spectral centroid, which rises with energy in upper harmonics. EQ can only boost what exists; saturation/exciters create new harmonics; octave layers add bright partials that are musically related.
prerequisites: DAW or the numpy renderer in sample-lab

outputs.name: result
outputs.description: Rendered part or recipe following the workflow

constraints: Portable recipe; not affiliated with any vendor; do not copy factory presets or sample packs.
Numbers in variants come from the source video transcripts; workflow steps are the consolidated mainstream practice.
Bring drums in early and avoid pitch wobble unless asked (user preferences from daily tests).

steps.action: Measure first: spectral centroid of the pad vs a reference (ambient pads ~1.5-3 kHz; dark tests sat ~0.8 kHz).
Oscillator: saw/supersaw or bright wavetable frames rather than sine/triangle; keep enough harmonics (no low-passed sources).
Filter: cutoff 3-6 kHz, key-tracking 50-100%, filter env to open on attack; avoid treble-cut on the pad.
Layer: octave-up sine/triangle or glock/bell partials at -12 to -18 dB; pluck/struck layers bring natural brightness.
Exciter: high-pass a copy at ~3 kHz, saturate (tanh/tube), blend -12 dB; or pitch-shift +12 in reverb (shimmer).
Air: high-passed noise >8 kHz at -24 to -30 dB following the pad envelope.
Brighten before reverb/delay (pre-send), not on the master; finish with a gentle 10-12 kHz shelf (+1-3 dB) only if needed.
Check harshness at 2-5 kHz and on small speakers; re-measure centroid.
Hear the theory: run `/home/box/audio-tools/bin/python sample-lab/theory/brightness_air.py` from the repo root and compare the sections; reuse its functions as a starting point for renders.
steps.expect: WAV in sample-lab/theory/out/ demonstrating the principle

verification: Render a short test and A/B against a reference at matched loudness
Run the generator and confirm it writes a WAV without error
Check mono compatibility and that no element masks the kick/bass

variants.name: Start-bright-then-filter pad: pick a harmonically rich (buzzy/bright) oscillator, odd unison 5-9, slow wavetable-position sweep, then low-pass to smooth it (keeping top-end headroom to automate back in), big low-cut reverb, low-cut EQ and a stereo imager to pull the pad around the listener; plus an attack-removed swell pad from any played source
variants.goal: Make smooth, lush ambient pads that can still get bright on demand: start from a source with lots of high harmonics and remove highs with a synth filter (not an end-of-chain EQ), so the cutoff can be automated to bring brightness and air back for tension. Delta vs the brightness cluster: the 'rich source -> filter -> space' order, odd vs even unison as solid vs unstable, imager after big reverb to bring a distant pad back around the ears, and volume-swelling any played source (guitar, piano, vocal) so the reverb is fed only by the tone, not the attack.
steps: Set amp attack and release to about 400-500 ms each as a starting point, then tailor to the part.
Choose a bright, buzzy, harmonically rich oscillator (a saw, or a PWM/analog-style wavetable). Try many; keep the one with the most high-end energy and character.

Unison: an odd voice count (5, 7 or 9) gives a solid centre voice with voices spread either side; below 5 is not lush, above 9 costs CPU. For a rougher 'organic' pad, use an even count (e.g. 4): no centre voice gives a slightly unstable, edgy quality. Detune stays static.
Optional motion: route a slow LFO or long envelope to wavetable position so it sweeps gently through the table.

Low-pass the tone inside the synth (12 or 18 dB/oct; 18 gives a more pronounced cutoff) until smooth, then raise volume to compensate. Use the filter rather than an EQ so the cutoff can be automated to reintroduce highs for builds.
Space: a very large reverb at high mix with plenty of low-cut (filter before or after reverb, either order works), then an EQ cutting excess low end and optionally a second reverb.
Add a stereo imager after the reverbs and A/B: without it the pad sits far in front; with it the pad wraps around the listener.

Swell variant: play chords or a melody on any source (guitar, piano, vocal), start slightly before the bar, and put a gain envelope first in the chain that rises from 0 at the bar so the attack is removed. Then low-cut EQ, imager, and reverb, which is now fed only by the swell.

variants.name: Ambient air layer from a field recording: HPF out traffic lows, subtle harmonic exciter for upper sparkle, light high-end lift; keep it subtle to avoid glassy mess
variants.goal: Add musical 'air' to an ambient/cinematic bed using a real field recording (birds, room tone, distant detail) instead of only filtering a bright synth: high-pass to remove traffic/human low-end pollution (which also cools the bed), then a subtle harmonic exciter / 'fresh air' style upper-band enhancer to restore sparkle and emphasize distant calls, optionally with a light high-shelf. Warn: easy to overdo into a glassy mess — keep excitation subtle. Delta vs brightness-and-air start-bright-then-filter-pad (bright oscillator → LPF inside synth): this is a parallel air/detail layer from recorded ambience + HPF + exciter, not source-brightness via filter.
steps: Place a field recording on its own track above the ambient bed. Solo and find the useful high detail (e.g. a bird call) and the muddy low end (traffic / human noise pollution).
High-pass the recording to remove the low-end pollution. Expect the bed to sound a bit colder/thinner — that is intended before air is restored.
Add a subtle harmonic exciter / upper-band enhancer ('fresh air' style) to excite upper frequencies so the clip sounds less dull and distant calls poke through. Keep the amount very low.
Optionally add a small high-end shelf/boost for the same emphasis. A/B against the bed; if it turns glassy or harsh, back off exciter then shelf.

Optional motion (same chain idea on a second ambience layer): duplicate with time-stretch/smear automation alternating wet/dry, and/or slow tremolo with changing rate that also pans L↔R for headphone width. Keep levels under the musical bed.

In the full mix, verify the air layer adds space above ~ several kHz without muddying the pad/drone. Use storytelling markers (a single call → larger event) if arranging a nature-to-elsewhere transition.

variants.name: Synth-native noise air: noise osc on its own low-pass with a fast envelope for bright attack, shelved tape-noise bed boosted near 6 kHz, +24 st noise layer on bass, envelope-following tuned noise on drums, parallel master noise chain
variants.goal: Add air and 'fidelity' with noise generated or layered inside the patch instead of opening the main filter (which adds unwanted energy). Core recipe: put noise on oscillator 2, route oscillators to separate filters (split routing), low-pass the noise and drive its cutoff from a sharp, fast envelope so it adds only a bright, breathy attack. Supporting layers: a low-shelved tape-noise bed with a bell boost near 6 kHz, sneaked in until barely noticed; a noise sampler on the bass MIDI transposed +24 st with a short decay at about -8 dB; envelope-following narrow-band noise on kick (~5 kHz) and snare (~7 kHz, decorrelated for width); and a parallel master noise chain after the other master FX with slow, unsynced, out-of-phase filter LFOs. Delta vs brightness-and-air variants (start-bright-then-filter, field-recording HPF+exciter): this one makes the air from noise inside the synth/patch and on each element.
steps: Noise bed: put a long tape-hiss/white-noise sample on its own track and hold one note for the whole section. Add an EQ with a low shelf turned down to clear masking lows (shelf, not a steep low cut), then a smooth bell boost around 6 kHz (the 'brilliance' range) where the noise sounds pleasant.
Pull the bed way down, then raise it until you just notice it. A/B: without it the mix should sound 'clinical/lifeless'; with it, a little fidelity comes back.
Synth-native air: in the pad/lead patch, turn on oscillator 2 with a noise wave. Set filter routing to split so osc 1 goes to filter 1 and the noise osc goes to filter 2.

Set filter 2 to low-pass. Give envelope 2 a sharp spike (fast attack, short decay, no sustain) and route it to filter 2 cutoff in the mod matrix. Lower filter 2's base cutoff until the noise is heard only as a bright, breathy attack, not a steady hiss. Turn resonance down.

Raise the envelope-to-cutoff amount for more punch, and back off the noise osc level so it isn't detectable as noise. Optionally automate the noise level up over a section as a slow, rising energy element.

Bass noise layer: group the bass chain and add a parallel chain with a white-noise sample in a sampler, fed by the same MIDI. Add a pitch MIDI effect of +24 semitones so the noise sits two octaves up and its colour follows the notes. Set amp envelope sustain to 0 and tune decay to a short burst; mix it at about -8 dB.

Drums: put an envelope-following tuned-noise device (noise shaped by the input's envelope, narrow band-pass; Erosion-like) on the kick around 5 kHz for snap, and on the snare around 7 kHz. For the snare, switch to decorrelated/wide noise (different L/R) for a stereo burst. The peak level rises, so turn the track down to keep limiter headroom.

Master noise: make a parallel rack on the master after the other master FX, with a dry chain and a noise chain. In the noise chain, use a noise generator (e.g. a delay's noise feature) with input at about -40 dB or none. Filter the noise and modulate the two filters with slow, unsynced LFOs set out of phase with each other, plus an optional small resonant hump. Sneak it in.
Map every noise addition to one mute/macro key and A/B the full mix with and without the noise.
